prompt: Put these in the order the course takes them.
hint: The problem comes before the algorithms, and production comes last.
items: The trivial rule a model has to beat
The leaks that make a test lie
The threshold as a business decision
A model behind an address, watched for drift
trap: Leakage sits in lesson 4, before any algorithm, because a leaking test makes every later comparison worthless.

prompt: Why does the course put framing, baselines, splits and leakage before any algorithm?
hint: Think about what a bad test does to a good-looking number.

choices.text: Because every algorithm from lesson 5 on imports the code those four lessons write, and cannot run without it
choices.why: Nothing in lesson 5 imports lesson 3. The reason is about trusting a score, not about code.

choices.text: Because they are the easiest material, and a course of ninety hours has to begin with the gentlest part
choices.why: They are easier to skip, not easier to get right. Leakage catches experienced people.

choices.text: Because a model judged on a leaking split, against no baseline, looks exactly like a good one
choices.why: Yes. Those four lessons decide whether any later number means anything.

choices.text: Because scikit-learn requires a baseline to be fitted first
choices.why: scikit-learn requires nothing of the kind. A baseline is a discipline, not an API rule.

prompt: What does the virtual environment in `~/ml/.venv` protect?
hint: Ask where the libraries are installed, and what else would otherwise share them.

choices.text: Your files in `~/ml`, from being read or changed by other users of the same computer
choices.why: An environment is not a permission. Anyone who could read `~/ml` still can.

choices.text: Every other Python on the machine, from these libraries
choices.why: Yes. Everything installed lives inside one folder, and deleting it removes the lab.

choices.text: The model, from changing between runs
choices.why: Pinned versions help with that; the environment is where they are pinned, not what keeps a model fixed.

choices.text: The processor, from fits that run too long
choices.why: Nothing about an environment limits computation.

prompt: `requirements.txt` says `scikit-learn==1.9.1` rather than just `scikit-learn`. What does the pin buy?
hint: A default inside a library is part of its behaviour.

choices.text: A licence to redistribute the library inside your own programs, which the unpinned name does not grant
choices.why: Licences have nothing to do with version numbers.

choices.text: Protection from the security problems that newer versions of a library tend to introduce
choices.why: Pinning freezes old problems as readily as it avoids new ones. The goal here is reproducibility.

choices.text: The same defaults, so the same program prints the same scores
choices.why: Yes. A changed default changes a score without a line of your code changing.

choices.text: A faster install, because pip skips the search
choices.why: pip still resolves and downloads; speed is not the reason.

prompt: Why is installing in a virtual environment the recommended path here, rather than a virtual machine?
hint: What does this course spend most of its time doing?

choices.text: Online notebooks are always free
choices.why: Their allowance belongs to a company that can change it, which is why the course depends on none of them.

choices.text: The course needs a graphics card
choices.why: It needs none. A processor is enough, which is the line between this course and the next.

choices.text: Virtual machines cannot run scikit-learn
choices.why: They run it perfectly well, and the transcripts match exactly inside one.

choices.text: A database server must run beside the code
choices.why: There is no database in this course.

choices.text: It would take processors and memory away from the fits
choices.why: Yes. And the environment changes nothing outside one folder, which removes the usual reason for a machine apart.

prompt: The line `export ___=1` in `~/.bashrc` stops activation from adding `(.venv)` to the prompt.
hint: Its name says what it disables.

prompt: `python3 make_data.py` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'`, and you installed NumPy ten minutes ago. What is the likely cause?
hint: There are two Pythons on the machine.

choices.text: NumPy's install failed in silence
choices.why: A failed pip install says so in red. Silence after `--quiet` is success.

choices.text: It ran the system's Python
choices.why: Yes. Activate the environment, or open a terminal that read the new `~/.bashrc` lines; `which python` confirms it.

choices.text: NumPy installs a compiled library that is only loaded after the computer restarts
choices.why: No Python library needs a restart.

choices.text: The data folder is missing
choices.why: That fails later, with a file error. This one fails at the first `import`.

prompt: pip answers `externally-managed-environment` and suggests `--break-system-packages`. What should you do?
hint: The message is protecting something.

choices.text: Run the same command with `sudo`
choices.why: That is the same change with more permission to make it.

choices.text: Activate `~/ml/.venv` and install there
choices.why: Yes. The environment is exactly what the message asks for.

choices.text: Pass the flag, since pip itself suggested it
choices.why: The name is accurate: it lets pip change the Python the system runs on, which can break the system.

prompt: pip says `No matching distribution found for scikit-learn==1.9.1` on a computer with Python 3.9. What is the first thing to check?
hint: The same message covers a misspelt name, a version that does not exist, and one that does not exist for you.

choices.text: Whether the disk is full
choices.why: A full disk fails while writing files, with a different error.

choices.text: The Python version
choices.why: Yes. The course needs Python 3.12 or newer, and `python3 --version` settles it.

choices.text: Whether the Python Package Index is down or refusing connections today
choices.why: An unreachable index produces a connection error, not this message.

choices.text: Whether scikit-learn was spelt `sklearn`
choices.why: The name in the message is spelt correctly. Read what pip quotes back.

prompt: Why does `make_data.py` start its random number generator with a fixed seed?
hint: Compare your numbers with the transcripts.

choices.text: So every computer writes identical files
choices.why: Yes. The checksums prove it: one wrong character in the paste changes a line.

choices.text: So the program runs faster
choices.why: Seeding costs nothing and saves nothing.

choices.text: Because NumPy refuses to generate random numbers at all until somebody gives it a seed
choices.why: Without a seed NumPy draws from the operating system's entropy, and the files would differ every run.

choices.text: So the data looks more realistic
choices.why: A seed does not change how realistic the draws are, only whether they repeat.

prompt: In `churn.csv`, what is one row?
hint: The same customer id appears many times.

choices.text: One subscriber on the first day of one month
choices.why: Yes, with the 90 days before it and whether they cancelled in the month after.

choices.text: One cancellation
choices.why: Most rows are people who stayed; `churned` is 0 in about 94% of them.

choices.text: One box delivered
choices.why: Deliveries are `deliveries.csv`.

choices.text: One subscriber, with everything known about them
choices.why: Then each id would appear once. 7,583 people fill 62,885 rows.

prompt: `churn.csv` has 62,885 rows and 7,583 distinct subscribers. On average, how many monthly snapshots does each subscriber have? Two decimal places.
hint: Rows divided by people.

prompt: Which of these is the decision the churn model exists to inform?
hint: A decision is something somebody does.

choices.text: Who gets the R$ 40 credit
choices.why: Yes. The prediction is worth something only through this.

choices.text: Which algorithm to use
choices.why: That is a choice inside the project, not the business decision it serves.

choices.text: What share of the subscribers cancelled in December, broken down by city
choices.why: That is a report about the past, and needs no model.

choices.text: Which subscribers will cancel
choices.why: That is the prediction. Nothing has been done yet.

prompt: Logistics wants to tell each customer how many minutes their box will take. What kind of problem is that?
hint: Look at what is predicted: a category, or a quantity?

choices.text: Regression
choices.why: Yes. The target is a quantity, and lesson 5 fits the first one.

choices.text: Classification, because the answer is on time or late
choices.why: That would be a different question. Here the target is `minutes`, a number.

choices.text: Clustering, because deliveries fall into groups
choices.why: Clustering has no target at all. Here there is one.

choices.text: Neither; it needs a neural network
choices.why: A neural network is one way to fit a regression, not a different kind of problem.

prompt: A credit costs R$ 40, keeps 30% of the people about to leave, and a kept subscriber is worth R$ 480. What is a credit sent to a true positive worth on average, in reais?
hint: Expected value kept, minus what the credit cost.

prompt: A subscriber receives the credit and was never going to cancel. Which outcome is that?
hint: Positive means the model said *cancel*.

choices.text: A false negative
choices.why: A negative is the model saying *stay*. Here it said cancel.

choices.text: A true positive
choices.why: True would mean they really were about to leave.

choices.text: A false positive
choices.why: Yes: the model said cancel, and it was wrong. R$ 40 given away.

choices.text: A true negative
choices.why: No credit goes out in a negative.

prompt: In December 4,146 subscribers were scored and 248 cancelled. If every one of them got the R$ 40 credit and 30% of the leavers were kept at R$ 480 each, what would the month net, in reais? Use a minus sign for a loss.
hint: 74.4 kept, against a credit for everybody.

prompt: A colleague reports a churn model worth R$ 40,000 a month in December, using the same costs and the same 248 leavers. What do you conclude?
hint: Work out what a perfect model would be worth.

choices.text: The model probably has a high precision
choices.why: Even a precision of 1 cannot exceed the ceiling.

choices.text: The costs should be raised to match the model
choices.why: The costs come from the business. They are not tuned to flatter a model.

choices.text: The arithmetic is wrong
choices.why: Yes. A perfect model is worth R$ 25,792 with these costs; a real one gets a fraction of that.

choices.text: The model is excellent and should go to production
choices.why: No model can beat sending exactly the 248 leavers the credit, and that is worth R$ 25,792.

prompt: Which of these are reasons NOT to build a model? Choose all that apply.
hint: Each condition in the section has a failure that comes from missing it.

choices.text: Cancellations are recorded only when somebody phones
choices.why: Yes. The label then means *phoned*, and a model learns to predict calls.

choices.text: A single rule of thumb already separates leavers perfectly
choices.why: Yes. Write the rule down; a model adds cost and nothing else.

choices.text: There are a few thousand labelled cancellations
choices.why: That is enough to learn from; 3,685 here.

choices.text: The list of who gets the credit is fixed by hand whatever the model says
choices.why: Yes. A prediction that changes no action is worth nothing.

choices.text: The signal is spread over a dozen columns
choices.why: That is exactly when a model earns its place.

prompt: A proposed feature is *complaints in the first week of the month*. The prediction is made on the first of the month. What is wrong with it?
hint: Ask when its value becomes known.

choices.text: It is not known yet on the first
choices.why: Yes. A week after the credit has gone out is too late to decide whether to send it.

choices.text: It should be a count over the last 90 days, like every other column in `churn.csv`
choices.why: The window length is a choice; a window that ends in the future is the error.

choices.text: Complaints are too rare to help
choices.why: Rare or not, the problem is earlier than that.

choices.text: Nothing, if it predicts well
choices.why: It will predict very well and be impossible to compute when it matters. Lesson 4 is about that.

prompt: Three months after launch, a manager complains that the model is "only 30% precise". What does the one-page frame let Ana answer?
hint: What did everybody agree the model was for?

choices.text: That the agreed goal was net value, and here it is
choices.why: Yes. The frame turns an argument about a metric into a reading of the agreed number.

choices.text: That the model will be retrained until precision passes 50%
choices.why: Chasing precision can lose money: fewer credits, fewer people kept.

choices.text: That precision is the wrong word, and accuracy is higher
choices.why: Swapping metrics is not an answer; the agreed goal is.

choices.text: That 30% is normal for churn models
choices.why: Normal elsewhere says nothing about whether it pays here.

prompt: Suppose the credit cost R$ 150 instead of R$ 40, everything else equal. What happens to the value of a credit sent to a true positive?
hint: 0.3 × 480 is the expected value kept.

choices.text: It falls but stays positive
choices.why: Work it out: 0.3 × 480 = 144, which is less than 150.

choices.text: It becomes negative, so even a perfect model should send nobody the credit
choices.why: Yes: 144 − 150 = −6. The decision, not the model, was the problem.

choices.text: It doubles, because the credit is more attractive
choices.why: The 30% is given and fixed in the question; nothing says it rises.

choices.text: It stays the same, because only false positives cost the credit
choices.why: Every credit sent costs its price, to whomever it goes.
